## The one-line version

`vi.useFakeTimers()` replaces the global timer functions, which silently disarms
**every** bound built on them — including bounds inside libraries you don't own.
A code path that touches real I/O (PG, sockets, fs with retries) then has *no
timeout at all* and hangs forever.

If you need fake timers around a path that touches real I/O:

```ts
vi.useFakeTimers({ shouldAdvanceTime: true });
```

Real I/O makes progress, and `vi.advanceTimersByTimeAsync` still works, so you
keep deterministic control of long waits. Both properties are pinned by
`libs/test-config/src/fake-timers-real-io-contract.test.ts` — if a Vitest or
`@sinonjs/fake-timers` upgrade breaks either, that file reds.

## Why this one is expensive to diagnose

The failure is a **hang**, not an assertion. Three things follow, and each one
sends you to the wrong place:

1. **It surfaces as somebody else's error.** You get `Hook timed out in 90000ms`
   or a killed worker, attributed to whatever hook or test happened to be
   running when the budget expired — often a `beforeAll`/`afterAll` that is
   completely innocent. It looks exactly like the load/teardown flake classes
   (EI-10634 timeout-budget asymmetry, EI-10726 unbounded `afterEach`), so the
   natural first move is to widen a timeout, which never helps.
2. **The bound that vanished is usually not in your file, or even our repo.**
   In the motivating case it was `postgres.js`'s internal query timer.
3. **Absence of a timeout produces no log line.** Nothing reports "the guard you
   were relying on is disarmed." The code just never continues.

## The motivating case (EI-18121952237624498) — and a warning about the first diagnosis

The real chain was:

```
buildHiveRekeyBootDeps      packages/operator-core/lib/sync/hyperbee/hive-epoch-boot-deps.ts:80
  → potHomeSlugForHarness   packages/operator-core/lib/hive-federation.ts:92   (its FIRST await)
    → loadHarnessRegistry   packages/operator-core/lib/harness-registry.ts:206
      → readOperatorState   → PG via postgres.js   ← the frozen bound
```

The comment originally documenting this in `wire-outbox.test.ts` blamed
`getFlag`'s `setTimeout`-based backend guard. **That was wrong**, and it is worth
knowing why, because the reasoning was superficially perfect: `getFlag` *does*
contain exactly such a guard (`withFlagBackendTimeout`, `libs/flags/src/server.ts`),
and fake timers *do* disarm it. Both premises are true. The conclusion still
failed, because in a unit-test process `getFlag` never reaches that guard: no
PostHog client is initialised and no flag override store is installed, so it
short-circuits to `FLAG_DEFAULTS` — measured at **0 ms** under fake timers on a
cold cache.

The generalisable lesson: *a plausible mechanism in a component you have read is
not evidence that this component ran.* Before accepting a mechanism, prove the
suspect code is actually reached and actually slow. Measure it; don't infer it.

## How to find which `await` is hanging

A hang gives you no stack, so convert it into a **labelled verdict** per
candidate step. Race each step against a deadline measured on a timer captured
*before* any fake-timer install:

```ts
// Captured at MODULE LOAD. Capturing this after vi.useFakeTimers() would capture
// the FAKE timer, the deadline would never fire, and every probe below would be
// vacuous — a hang would present as an infinite hang instead of a verdict.
const PRISTINE_SET_TIMEOUT = globalThis.setTimeout;

const hatch = <T,>(p: Promise<T>, ms: number, label: T) =>
  Promise.race([
    p,
    new Promise<T>((res) => {
      PRISTINE_SET_TIMEOUT(() => res(label), ms);
    }),
  ]);
```

Then walk the call chain one level at a time, innermost suspect last:

```ts
it('does X hang?', async () => {
  vi.useFakeTimers();
  const v = await hatch(candidateStep().then((r) => `resolved:${r}`), 4000, 'HUNG');
  console.info('VERDICT:', v);
  expect(v).not.toBe('HUNG');
});
```

Each step returns `resolved:…` or `HUNG`, and the first `HUNG` is your culprit.
This is the same stage-count funnel idea used for silent detectors: instrument
every stage and find where the value collapses.

**Always include a control arm** — the same call under *real* timers, which must
resolve. Without it, a `HUNG` verdict is ambiguous between "fake timers froze it"
and "this call is just broken/slow here". In the motivating case the control
(`resolved:deps` in 773 ms on real timers) is what made the diagnosis airtight.

### Two traps that make the probe lie

- **Capturing the pristine timer too late.** Capture it at module load. Mutating
  the contract test to capture it lazily makes the probe hang for the full 60 s
  test timeout instead of reporting in 250 ms — verified.
- **Cache warming across tests.** If an earlier test in the file already called
  the function under real timers, a later fake-timer call may hit a warm cache
  and resolve instantly, which reads as "no hang" and exonerates the wrong
  component. Run the cold-cache fake-timer probe **first**, or isolate the file.

## Ruling out the look-alikes

All three present as `Hook timed out`. Distinguish before fixing:

| Class | Tell | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Frozen real-I/O bound** (this doc) | Test uses `vi.useFakeTimers()` *and* the path touches PG/fs/sockets. Hangs indefinitely; real-timer control arm passes. | `{ shouldAdvanceTime: true }`, or don't fake timers on that path. |
| **Timeout-budget asymmetry** (EI-10634) | `beforeAll` has bespoke headroom, `afterAll` inherits the default. Fails near a budget boundary, worse under fleet load. | Align the hook budgets. |
| **Unbounded teardown** (EI-10726) | Hand-rolled `afterEach` cleanup loop with no bound. | Use the shared rig teardown helper. |

## What NOT to do

Widening the timeout, `--no-threads`, retrying the file, or hand-advancing
timers at one call site are all mitigations: they leave the disarmed bound in
place for the next path that reaches it. Fix which clock the test installs.

Equally, do **not** "harden" the product code against this — adding a
fake-timer-proof bound (e.g. `AbortSignal.timeout`, which sinon does not fake) to
`withFlagBackendTimeout` or `loadHarnessRegistry` would be changing production
code to accommodate a test-only condition. Nothing fakes timers in production;
`postgres.js` keeps its real bounds there. The defect is in the test's choice of
clock, so that is where the fix belongs.
